title: 1951 Atlantic C-124 disappearance
summary: The C-124 transport reported a fire in the cargo hold and ditched successfully into the Atlantic Ocean. The aircraft landed safely and intact in the water and all occupants donned life preservers and climbed into inflatable rafts with survival supplies. However, when rescue vessel USS Casco arrived at the ditching location, the aircraft and all 53 occupants had disappeared; only charred plywood and a briefcase were found.
probable_cause: The aircraft successfully ditched in the Atlantic after reporting a cargo hold fire that could not be extinguished. All hands were recovered in life rafts with survival equipment. The fate of the aircraft and crew remains unknown; no bodies or significant wreckage was recovered.

factors.evidence: aircraft radioed Mayday reporting a fire in the cargo crates

All hands donned life preservers and climbed into inflatable 5-man rafts equipped with survival supplies

events.text: Aircraft radioed Mayday to weather ship USCGC Casco reporting a fire in the cargo crates

When rescue vessel arrived at ditching location on 24 March, aircraft and all occupants had disappeared; only charred plywood and a briefcase found

notes: Successful ditching but subsequent disappearance of all occupants; cause of disappearance unknown; wreckage location never determined

title: Cubana de Aviación 493
summary: A Cubana de Aviación DC-4 and a US Navy Beechcraft SNB-1 collided in mid-air over Key West in clear weather conditions. Both aircraft were operating under visual flight rules. The SNB-1 had taken off from Naval Air Station Key West for instrument training. The CAA determined both crews failed to exercise due vigilance in looking for and avoiding conflicting traffic.
probable_cause: Failure on the parts of both air crews to exercise due vigilance in looking for and avoiding conflicting traffic.

title: Pan Am 151
summary: During pre-dawn approach to Monrovia, crew reported Dakar beacon interference with Robertsfield beacon. Aircraft descended below minimum altitude and crashed into hill at 1050 ft elevation. Investigation determined aircraft was beyond beacon's effective range and captain descended without positive position identification.
probable_cause: Captain descending below en route minimum altitude without positive identification of flight position.

title: United Airlines 610
summary: United Airlines Flight 610 descended from Salt Lake City to Denver on a transcontinental route on June 30, 1951. After requesting a lower altitude to 8,500 feet near Cheyenne, the captain selected incorrect audio frequency switches in the darkened cockpit, receiving Denver Visual Audio Range signals instead of the proper Denver low frequency range signals. The aircraft maintained a 210-degree intercept heading without hearing the required 'N' identifier signal to turn toward the destination. At 2:00 a.m., the aircraft crashed into Crystal Mountain, killing all 50 aboard.
probable_cause: The pilot selected incorrect audio frequency selector switches in a darkened cockpit, providing VAR course signals instead of low frequency range signals, preventing receipt of the navigation signal needed to turn toward the destination.

Turned to heading of approximately 210 degrees to intercept 168-degree course line
DC-6 crashed into Crystal Mountain and skidded 690 feet before bursting into flames

title: United Airlines 615
summary: United Air Lines Flight 615, a Douglas DC-6, crashed into mountainous terrain 15 miles southeast of Oakland on August 24, 1951 while on approach. The pilot ignored prescribed instrument landing procedures and instead relied on visual reference using the copilot's automatic direction finder. The ADF threw the plane 3 miles off course and below the prescribed altitude of 3,500 feet. The aircraft careened into Tolman Peak and over its knoll, scattering on the downslope. All 50 persons on board perished.
probable_cause: Pilot ignored the prescribed instrument landing procedures and relied instead on visual reference using the copilot's automatic direction finder, which threw the plane off course and below the prescribed altitude.

title: 1951 Miami Airlines C-46 crash
summary: A Miami Airlines Curtiss C-46 crashed in Elizabeth, New Jersey, shortly after taking off from Newark Airport on 16 December 1951, killing all 56 people on board. The right engine caught fire during takeoff; smoke was observed by ATC and ground personnel. The crew attempted to lower the landing gear when warned, but fire spread progressively. The aircraft crashed into buildings and the Elizabeth Water Company property. Investigation determined that hold-down studs of the right engine's number 10 cylinder had failed, setting off the fire that brought down the aircraft.
probable_cause: Hold-down studs of the right engine's number 10 cylinder failed, setting off the fire
